# The games layer

The games layer adds to the GNU root what games need beyond the desktop: innoextract, which unpacks Inno Setup installers such as GOG's offline installers, on both architectures, and on x86-64 the native games SuperTuxKart and 0 A.D. with their fixed replays, which measure their frame times, and the game launcher, `rach2-game`, with umu-launcher and the Steam Linux Runtime it runs Proton in. Its Debian packages are a closure of their own, from the snapshot and keys of the [Debian layer](../debian/Readme.md), installed after the desktop closure, so that the programs and settings the games tasks add have one directory and one install script.

## Use

`innoextract -d DIR SETUP.exe` unpacks an installer and the `SETUP-N.bin` files beside it into `DIR`; `innoextract --list` lists its files and `--version` prints the program's version and the formats it reads. Debian's page is rendered on the machine as `man innoextract`.

### Native games

On x86-64, `supertuxkart` starts SuperTuxKart 1.4, a kart racer, and `0ad` starts 0 A.D. 0.27.0, a real-time strategy game, whose engine is `pyrogenesis`. Both are in `/usr/games`, as Debian puts them, which `/etc/profile.d/games.sh` adds to the path of every login shell, after the rest. Each keeps its settings, saves and caches under the user's `~/.config`, `~/.local/share` and `~/.cache`. Debian's pages are `man supertuxkart` and `man 0ad`.

The x86-64 root's i386 layer adds the i386 SuperTuxKart, Debian's `supertuxkart:i386` of the same version, as `/usr/games/supertuxkart.i386-linux-gnu`, the name `mesa-utils-bin` gives its i386 programs, since dpkg keeps one architecture's `/usr/games/supertuxkart`. It reads the same data, `supertuxkart-data`, which has no architecture, and draws through the i386 Mesa; it plays the same benchmark race, and `man supertuxkart.i386-linux-gnu` is the same page. A root made with `GNU_I386=0` has no such game.

[`replays/`](replays) holds the fixed replays, installed at `/usr/share/games/rach2/replays`, which [`tests/graphics/runners/games.sh`](../../../tests/graphics/runners/games.sh) plays to measure each game's frame times, in QEMU and on the Lenovo. They are the replays of Linux's reference runs on the Lenovo, [`tools/lenovo/debian-ref/games.sh`](../../../tools/lenovo/debian-ref/games.sh), whose `mac.sh push` sends this directory, so that Rach2's numbers and Linux's are of the same play:

* [`supertuxkart.args`](replays/supertuxkart.args): the arguments of SuperTuxKart's profile mode, its benchmark: four AI karts on the hacienda track for 90 s of the race's own time from seed 1, after which the game ends itself and prints its profile summary.
* [`0ad-mainland/commands.txt`](replays/0ad-mainland/commands.txt), SHA-256 `36b46ada9217b79cdd8cf4dbe04d65dcec2b621df02ab440186531e564bc26db`: 39,701 turns of a match on the random map Mainland, size 192, seeds 1, Athenians against Britons, two Petra AI players and the player an observer, with no victory condition, recorded on the Lenovo by `games.sh record`, a non-visual autostart that ran 240 s. A replay holds the match's settings and each player's commands, of which an AI's are none, since a replay runs the AI players again; `0ad -replay-visual=commands.txt` plays it, and is ended 150 s after its loading screen.

### Proton

On x86-64, `rach2-game [--id ID] [--prefix DIR] [--] PROGRAM [ARGUMENT...]` runs a Windows program through `/opt/proton/proton run`, without Steam. `--id` chooses a decimal game ID (the inherited `SteamGameId`, or 0); give each game its own ID or prefix. The default compatibility directory is `$XDG_DATA_HOME/rach2/games/ID`, or `$HOME/.local/share/rach2/games/ID`; Proton keeps its Wine prefix under `pfx` there. `--prefix` chooses that compatibility directory, not its `pfx` child. An inherited `STEAM_COMPAT_DATA_PATH` also chooses it. The directories must be absolute paths. The launcher creates them only when it runs a program; `--print` prints the settings without creating a prefix or starting Proton.

The route sets `PROTON_USE_WOW64=1`, `PROTON_USE_WINED3D=1` and `WINE_D3D_CONFIG=renderer=gl`: GE-Proton11-12's WoW64 and WineD3D on OpenGL, which runs on llvmpipe in QEMU and Crocus on Haswell. `PROTON_NO_FSYNC=0` leaves fsync on, including when the calling shell disabled it. Proton then sets `WINEFSYNC=1`; its Wine tests the kernel's futex support. The launcher sets both `SteamGameId` and `SteamAppId` to the ID and `PROTON_LOG=1`, since Proton writes no log without `SteamGameId`. The log is `steam-ID.log` under `PROTON_LOG_DIR`, which defaults to `logs` in the compatibility directory. Proton replaces that log on each launch. `PULSE_LATENCY_MSEC` is 60 unless the caller set it: libpulse then asks PulseAudio to hold 60 ms of each of Wine's streams in place of the 30 ms Wine asks for, and PulseAudio raises that to 158 ms, over the 128 ms its sink on `/dev/dsp` holds (the measurements end the section [Weston](#weston)). `STEAM_COMPAT_CLIENT_INSTALL_PATH` defaults to a directory named `steam` beside the default game directories; it supplies Proton's required client path without installing Steam. An inherited value is kept.

A compatibility directory without `pfx/user.reg` is new: the launcher first runs `wineboot -u` through Proton, which makes the prefix with its 32-bit `drive_c/windows/syswow64`, and prints `rach2-game: prefix: made DIR` before the program starts; a failed `wineboot` exits with status 1. WineD3D takes the video memory from the GL driver's `GLX_MESA_query_renderer`, as under Linux, so the launcher sets no `VideoMemorySize`. On virgl that size is the host's dedicated memory in KiB read as MiB: 16,430,080 MiB in the Debian guest and on Rach2 on the testing PC, whose RTX 4080 SUPER has 16,045 MiB, as `glxinfo -B` shows in its `Video memory` and `Dedicated video memory` lines (`dev-log/upstream.md`). A Direct3D 9 program sees at most 4,095 MiB of it, since `GetAvailableTextureMem` returns 32 bits.

### umu

`rach2-game --umu` runs the same route through umu-launcher's `umu-run` in the container of Steam Linux Runtime 4.0, steamrt4, which GE-Proton11-12's `toolmanifest.vdf` requires as app 4183110, as games run outside Steam under Linux. The launcher sets `PROTONPATH=/opt/proton`, `GAMEID=umu-ID`, from which umu sets `SteamGameId` and `SteamAppId` to the ID, `WINEPREFIX` to the compatibility directory and `UMU_RUNTIME_UPDATE=0`; `--print` adds them and `UMU_RUNTIME`, the runtime's directory. The prefix is made as on the direct route, through umu. umu sets `STEAM_COMPAT_DATA_PATH` to `WINEPREFIX` and links `pfx` in it to the directory itself, unless `pfx` is already a directory, as in a compatibility directory the direct route made. It sets `STEAM_COMPAT_CLIENT_INSTALL_PATH` to the empty string.

umu keeps the runtime in `$XDG_DATA_HOME/umu/steamrt4`, or `$HOME/.local/share/umu/steamrt4`, and would download it from Valve's servers when it is missing and update it on each start. The root has the pinned runtime's archive instead, `/opt/umu/SteamLinuxRuntime_4.tar.xz`, with its `VERSIONS.txt` beside it. When the user's copy has no `VERSIONS.txt` or a different one, the launcher unpacks the archive there under umu's own lock, `umu.lock` beside it, replacing the old copy, and prints `rach2-game: umu: unpacked the Steam Linux Runtime VERSION in DIR`. umu's first start checks the copy against its mtree with pressure-vessel's `pv-verify` and records that with `.installed.ok`, as after a download; a later start unpacks and downloads nothing. The copy is the user's own, on the file system of the user's home, since pressure-vessel builds each container's `/usr` in the runtime's `var` with hard links to the runtime's files, and falls back to copying them when it cannot link them, as across file systems.

pressure-vessel starts the game in new user and mount namespaces with its own bubblewrap, `srt-bwrap`, and passes in the X11 socket, `/dev/dri`, the PulseAudio socket of `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` and the D-Bus buses. It shares the home directory, the game's directory, which umu gives as `STEAM_COMPAT_INSTALL_PATH`, and the paths `PRESSURE_VESSEL_FILESYSTEMS_RW` lists, separated by colons. `STEAM_LINUX_RUNTIME_LOG=1` writes its log to `slr-*.log` in `STEAM_LINUX_RUNTIME_LOG_DIR`, or in `var` of the runtime.

The pinned DXVK and vkd3d-proton are outside this game route. Under Linux on the Lenovo's HD 4400, hasvk reports Vulkan 1.2.305: DXVK 3.1.1 refuses it for Vulkan 1.3 and then, with that check bypassed, `shaderInt16`; vkd3d-proton 3.1 refuses it for `maintenance5` and `maintenance6`. Venus between the program and hasvk does not remove the refusals. The second discovery run's report, 2026-11-08 to 09, section "Step 10: Venus through QEMU on the HD 4400", records them, with the raw output at `step10/probes-detail.txt`. WineD3D's Vulkan renderer drew small programs under Linux but crashed in Crysis as its timedemo started (the same report, step 8); the game route therefore uses its GL renderer.

### Crysis

On x86-64, `crysis.sh install SETUP.exe` installs the English GOG Crysis 2.0.0.7 build on `/data`, which must already be an ext2 file system mounted writable. Run it as the user who will play, after an administrator creates `/data/crysis` for that user. Keep `setup_crysis_2.0.0.7_(84418).exe` and its `-1.bin` and `-2.bin` beside each other. The command checks all three against `crysis-installers.sha256`, extracts with innoextract into a temporary directory on the data partition, selects the 2,358 files of `game.sha256`, and checks them before renaming the tree to `/data/crysis/game`. The language file comes from `__support/app/Game/Localized/Default.lng`; the other files have their manifest paths in innoextract's output. GOG's support installer and Galaxy helper are left out. An error removes the temporary extraction, and an existing game directory is refused. `crysis.sh verify` checks the installed files again; logs the game adds are outside the manifest.

`crysis.sh run [--umu] [--32] [--prefix DIR] [ARGUMENT...]` starts `Bin64/Crysis.exe -dx9` through `rach2-game`, with `Bin64` as its working directory and game ID 17300. `--umu` starts it through umu, with `/data/crysis/game` as `STEAM_COMPAT_INSTALL_PATH`, since umu maps drive S: to the directory above it and the game finds no language from the root of S:, and with `/data` added to `PRESSURE_VESSEL_FILESYSTEMS_RW`. `--32` starts the 32-bit `Bin32/Crysis.exe` under WoW64. `--prefix DIR` chooses another compatibility directory under `/data`, which the launcher makes on its first use. It adds `-userpath Z:\data\crysis\saves` for the game's profiles and saves. The compatibility directory is `/data/crysis/compat`, Mesa's shader cache `/data/crysis/cache/mesa`, Proton's logs `/data/crysis/logs`, and its Steam client directory `/data/crysis/steam`. It enables Mesa's on-disk cache even when the calling shell disabled it; `MESA_SHADER_CACHE_SHOW_STATS=true` asks Mesa to report hits and misses. The game and all these paths survive a root update because the data partition is left alone. Each user needs write access to the game tree too, since Crysis writes its game and benchmark logs there. No game files are part of a system image; the image stages only the script and hash manifests under `/usr/share/rach2/crysis`.

## Sources and license

On x86-64, [`umu.list`](umu.list) pins umu-launcher and the runtime by SHA-256, and `make gnu-games` runs [`fetch_umu.sh`](fetch_umu.sh), which fetches each into the clone's `build/cache/gnu` once, checks it on every use, checks that the zipapp is umu-launcher 1.4.4 and that the archive's `VERSIONS.txt` names the pinned build, and stages both under `umu/opt/umu` in the GNU build tree:

| Pin | Version | Source | Download | Installed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| umu-launcher | 1.4.4 | its release's `umu-launcher-1.4.4-zipapp.tar` on GitHub | 430,080 bytes | `/opt/umu/umu-run`, 419,388 bytes |
| Steam Linux Runtime 4.0 (steamrt4) | 4.0.20261021.265997, pressure-vessel 0.20261007.0 | `SteamLinuxRuntime_4.tar.xz` in `steamrt4/images/4.0.20261021.265997/` of repo.steampowered.com | 175,077,288 bytes | the archive itself; 711,197,917 bytes in 8,021 entries in each user's copy |

umu-launcher is under the GNU General Public License version 3; its zipapp bundles urllib3, truststore and six, under the MIT license, and python-xlib, under the LGPL 2.1 or later. The runtime is built from Debian 13.7 packages and Valve's steam-runtime-tools, pressure-vessel among them, each under its own license; the same image directory has their sources under `sources/`.

[`layer.list`](layer.list) names the packages, in the Debian layer's list format, each pinned to the version Debian's snapshot has. `make gnu-games` runs `../debian/fetch_debs.sh games` on it, which checks the snapshot's signed indices and every package by its SHA-256, as for the desktop. The stage is `debian/games` in the GNU build tree, with its closure and file lists under `work/debian/games`. [`native.list`](native.list) names the native games' packages, each with the selector `amd64`, so that the i686 root, which has no 4.1 GB to spare for their data, has none of them. [`i386.list`](i386.list) names the i386 SuperTuxKart, which `make ARCH=x86_64 gnu-i386` resolves with the [i386 layer](../Readme.md#the-i386-layer)'s list against the i386 indices, with `GNU_DEBIAN_UNFOLLOWED=supertuxkart-data`, so that the data package, 628 MB, is not fetched a second time; its closure adds 30 i386 packages, 14.1 MB, to the layer's, all of them Multi-Arch `same` libraries but the game, `libopenal-data`, `lsb-base`, `sysvinit-utils` and `x11-common`, which the amd64 closures supply at the same versions. innoextract 1.9-0.1+b1 is under the zlib license, and Boost's libraries are mostly under the Boost Software License 1.0. SuperTuxKart 1.4+dfsg-5+b1 is under the GPL version 3 or later, and its data, `supertuxkart-data` 1.4+dfsg-5, under the licenses its notice lists for each file, the GPL and Creative Commons licenses among them. 0 A.D. 0.27.0-2+b1 is under the GPL version 2 or later, and its data, `0ad-data` and `0ad-data-common` 0.27.0-1, under CC BY-SA 3.0. Each package keeps its notice at `/usr/share/doc/PACKAGE/copyright`; [`../debian/copyright`](../debian/copyright) has the programs'. The replays are Rach2's records of the games' play. The rebuilt Weston of [Weston](#weston) is under the MIT license, as Debian's is, and Rach2's patches are under the same.

## Design

`install_root.sh` sources [`install_games.sh`](install_games.sh) once the desktop closure, Venus, the i386 layer, Proton and the test suites are in the tree, before the agents layer. It installs the games closure as the desktop's is installed: a package of `SKIP` is left out, and so is one the desktop closure installed at the same version, while one it installed at another version, or a file the root already has, stops the image. innoextract's closure is the program and Boost 1.83's filesystem, iostreams and program options libraries; the C and C++ runtimes, zlib, bzip2, liblzma and zstd it needs are the GNU ports'. Since nothing resolved the closure against the root, the script then refuses the image when a library that an ELF file of the layer needs is in none of the loader's directory, `/lib`, `/usr/lib`, `/usr/lib/MULTIARCH` and the directories of the file's own RUNPATH or RPATH, with `$ORIGIN` taken as the file's directory: 0 A.D.'s engine finds SpiderMonkey 115, NVIDIA's texture tools and its editor's libraries in `/usr/lib/games/0ad` so, and names the loader itself, which resolves its own name. The games add 4.1 GB to the x86-64 root, 3.4 GB of it 0 A.D.'s data in one archive, `public.zip`, which the game reads in place. Beside the desktop closure and innoextract's their own brings SDL2, OpenAL, wxWidgets 3.2 for 0 A.D.'s editor, curl's GnuTLS build, enet, gloox, AngelScript, shaderc and some fonts. Debian's `libcurl4t64` and `libssh2-1t64`, which wxWidgets and curl's GnuTLS build need, are in the root's SKIP list, so that the curl and libssh2 ports' `libcurl.so.4` and `libssh2.so.1` serve them: glibc's loader takes a library that defines no symbol versions for a reference to a versioned symbol. The script copies `replays/` to `/usr/share/games/rach2/replays` and writes `/etc/profile.d/games.sh` when the root has `/usr/games`. With the i386 layer it copies the i386 closure's `/usr/games/supertuxkart` to `/usr/games/supertuxkart.i386-linux-gnu`, after checking that the games closure has `supertuxkart` at the version the i386 closure has, so that its data matches the program, and refuses the root when a library the program needs is not in `/usr/lib/i386-linux-gnu`.

### Wine in QEMU

[`tests/system/games/`](../../../tests/system/games) runs the pinned GE-Proton's Wine through `rach2-game` on the GNU root under QEMU's `virgl` profile, and the same runner, with the launcher from the payload, in the Debian 13 guest under the same profile, whose results are [`ref/linux.json`](../../../tests/system/games/ref/linux.json). [`run.py`](../../../tests/system/games/run.py) starts a headless Weston of its own on its GL renderer with Xwayland, as an ordinary user in the `render` group, `desktop` on Rach2 and `gfx` in Debian, and requires Weston's renderer to be virgl, or the one `GAMES_RENDERER` names. Weston gives Xwayland the render node through linux-dmabuf, so Xwayland offers DRI3 and Wine's GLX runs on virgl directly; under the Pixman renderer Xwayland has no GL of its own and GLX falls back to llvmpipe. Each row makes a new prefix in a private directory and removes it, with Weston and the Wine server, on every exit.

Its shell is desktop-shell, so that the guest's stock Weston, which has kiosk-shell's fault of [Weston](#weston), and Rach2's rebuilt one run the probes alike.

The probes are small Windows programs, each built 64-bit and 32-bit with MinGW in the Debian builder guest. `glprobe` makes a WGL context on a visible window, draws a triangle with red, green and blue corners over a navy clear into a 64x64 framebuffer object, reads it back and then draws and swaps the window; `d3d9probe` draws the same into a 64x64 Direct3D 9 render target, reads it back and presents it; each prints the CRC-32 of the readback's R, G, B and A bytes, row by row from the top. `holdprobe` waits until a file appears, so that the runner can read its `/proc/PID/maps`. `tripprobe` creates a Direct3D 11 device and 1000 times clears a 64x64 target, copies it to a staging texture and maps it, and prints the time, the test of the second graphics run under Linux on the Lenovo. The 32-bit programs run under WoW64, the route's, so their Unix side is the 64-bit preloader and loader.

In Debian, the GL probe names `virgl (D3D12 (NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4080 SUPER))`, OpenGL 4.2 compatibility on Mesa 25.0.7, and Direct3D 9 the adapter `Red Hat VirtIO GPU`, vendor 0x1af4, device 0x1010. Both widths read back the same pixels: GL `0017e166`, Direct3D 9 `3f9a06f0`. The prefix of 7,947 MiB of `MemTotal` gets `VideoMemorySize` 7947, and WineD3D's `trace+d3d` log reports `Use 7947MiB = 0x1f0b00000 bytes for emulated_textureram` and `Emulating 0x1f0b00000 bytes`; the Direct3D 9 probe sees 4,095 MiB.

Wine 11's preloader reserves four ranges of a 64-bit process (`loader/preloader.c`, `preload_info`): the DOS area at 0x10000, 1 MiB; the low area at 0x110000, 0x67ef0000 bytes; the 32-bit top-down area with the shared user data at 0x7f000000, 0xff0000 bytes; and the 64-bit top-down area with the virtual heap at 0x7ffffe000000, 0x1ff0000 bytes. In Debian a WoW64 process keeps all four mapped whole. A 64-bit process keeps only the 64-bit top-down area whole: Wine gives the low ranges back and maps only what it places there, 987,136 bytes of the DOS area, 6,930,432 of the low area and 2,162,688 of the 32-bit top-down area, NLS tables, heaps and the shared user data among them ([`ref/linux-hold64.maps`](../../../tests/system/games/ref/linux-hold64.maps), [`ref/linux-hold32.maps`](../../../tests/system/games/ref/linux-hold32.maps)).

Rach2 gives the same results under the same profile, 4 CPUs and 8 GiB: GL on virgl with the same renderer string, both probes at both widths with Linux's CRC-32s, and in each of the four ranges, for both programs, the bytes Linux maps. Its prefix gets `VideoMemorySize` 8173, its own `MemTotal`, and WineD3D reports that size. The `prefix` case took 165 s with its boot, and the other three, run at once, 173 s.

### Weston

The desktop session's Weston runs kiosk-shell, which shows one window at a time over the whole output; Rach2 rebuilds Debian's Weston 14.0.2-1 with five fixes for the games route, so that a fullscreen X client, a Windows program among them, sits at the output's origin, unframed and focused, captures the pointer, and a lower display mode fills the output.

Where an X window lands is decided by Weston's Xwayland window manager, `xwayland/window-manager.c`. A window it counts as fullscreen gets no frame margin: `weston_wm_window_get_frame_size` (lines 663 to 678) and `weston_wm_window_get_child_position` (lines 681 to 695) give it the window's own size and an offset of 0,0. Any other undecorated window gets the theme's margin, 32 pixels (`shared/cairo-util.c:433`) on each side, so its frame is 64 pixels larger and the client sits at 32,32 inside it: that is the +32+32. On desktop-shell a window is fullscreen when it sets `_NET_WM_STATE_FULLSCREEN` or when `legacy_fullscreen` (lines 3190 to 3232) recognises it: an override-redirect window at an output's place and size, or an undecorated one with `PPosition` at an output's origin and `PSize`, `USSize` or equal `PMinSize` and `PMaxSize` of the output's size. Wine's fullscreen window has `PPosition` 0,0 with static gravity, Motif hints that turn the decorations off, `WM_TAKE_FOCUS` and no size hint, since Wine counts a fullscreen window as resizable; it is fullscreen there only through the `_NET_WM_STATE_FULLSCREEN` it sets, and desktop-shell then puts it below its panel, at 0,32. An X client that sets neither, such as `tests/system/games/xplace.c`, gets the margin: on desktop-shell its frame is at -32,-32, 1430x832. kiosk-shell needs neither: `desktop_surface_added` (`kiosk-shell/kiosk-shell.c:851`) makes every toplevel fullscreen, so Wine's window and xplace's both sit at 0,0 at the output's size with no frame, once kiosk-shell centres them as below. Rach2 therefore keeps kiosk-shell and changes neither Wine nor its hints.

Five faults of Weston's stood in the way, and [`weston/`](weston) patches each:

* [`kiosk-active-tree.patch`](weston/kiosk-active-tree.patch): kiosk-shell freed a surface while an output still held its tree as the active one, and the next window to map walked the freed list; Weston died of a segmentation fault as Wine mapped a window after another went away (`dev-log/upstream.md`). The patch clears each output's active tree that points at a surface as the surface is destroyed.
* [`kiosk-fullscreen-centre.patch`](weston/kiosk-fullscreen-centre.patch): kiosk-shell centred a fullscreen surface only when it mapped or changed size, and told the window manager a view's place only from the view's transform signal once it was mapped. The window manager frames an X window that sets no fullscreen state with the margin until kiosk-shell makes it fullscreen, so its first commit is at its framed size, 1430x832, and a view centred while unmapped, or centred again where it was, sent no place: the X frame kept -32,-32, where it sat with its margin, while the screen showed the window at 0,0. The patch centres a fullscreen surface on each commit and reports an X window's place after each commit.
* [`xwm-emulated-mode.patch`](weston/xwm-emulated-mode.patch): Xwayland emulates a lower mode that an X client sets through RandR, lists it in `_XWAYLAND_RANDR_EMU_MONITOR_RECTS` on the client's windows and scales a window of that size at the output's origin to the output through `wp_viewport`, as Mutter lets it. Weston's window manager resized such a window to the output when kiosk-shell made it fullscreen, and kiosk-shell centred the smaller surface, so neither condition held. The patch reads the property, gives a fullscreen window the emulated size in its configure, keeps its X position at the output's origin, fullscreens it again when the property changes, and takes input over the whole scaled surface. Wine needs none of this: GE-Proton keeps its X window at the output's size and scales a lower mode itself, reporting the lower size to the program.
* [`xwm-mapped-managed.patch`](weston/xwm-mapped-managed.patch): Wine creates its fullscreen window override-redirect and makes it an ordinary window before mapping it. The window manager kept the flag it read at the window's creation, so it framed and showed the window but never gave it the input focus, which stayed None. A MapRequest comes only for a window that is not override-redirect, and the patch clears the flag there.
* [`pointer-constraint-view.patch`](weston/pointer-constraint-view.patch): a pointer constraint on a fullscreen surface was enabled at once on the pointer's focus view, whatever it was. A game that confines the pointer as it starts asks before Weston has painted its window, while the focus is still kiosk-shell's background view under it. The confine and lock grabs never pick the focus again, and the confine grab's motion handler asserts that the focus is a view of the constrained surface (`libweston/input.c:5719`), so Weston aborted at the mouse's next move. The patch starts the constraint on the focus only when it is a view of the constrained surface, and otherwise on the surface's first mapped view, which takes the focus; while the surface has no mapped view the constraint waits, as any other does.
* [`version.patch`](weston/version.patch) makes `weston --version` print `weston 14.0.2 (Rach2 14.0.2-1+rach2.1: kiosk-active-tree, kiosk-fullscreen-centre, xwm-emulated-mode, xwm-mapped-managed, pointer-constraint-view)`.

[`sources.txt`](weston/sources.txt) pins Debian's source package of the snapshot the desktop closure comes from, by SHA-256. `make ARCH=x86_64 gnu-weston` runs [`build_weston.sh`](weston/build_weston.sh), which boots the Debian builder guest of [`tests/graphics/debian-ref`](../../../tests/graphics/debian-ref), adds the patches that [`series`](weston/series) lists to the package's own, names the version 14.0.2-1+rach2.1 in a changelog entry of a fixed date, and builds the binary packages with Debian's rules and flags, without their tests. The host checks the `weston` and `libweston-14-0` packages against [`debs.sha256`](weston/debs.sha256), so a build that gives other bytes stops, and unpacks them into `weston/` of the GNU build tree. On an x86-64 Linux host, where the builder guest runs, `os-real-gnu.ext2` and `gnu-test.ext2` are made with `GNU_WESTON=1`, and `install_games.sh` removes every file the desktop closure's two packages installed and puts the rebuilt ones in their place; a root made in the tooling machine keeps Debian's.

In the desktop session on QEMU's `virgl` profile, xplace and Wine's Direct3D 9 fullscreen probe each sit at 0,0 at the output's 1366x768 with no frame, with focus and `_NET_WM_STATE_FULLSCREEN`, and the screen shows each window's halves from edge to edge; xplace's pointer grab, taken at the window's first Expose and confined to it, holds, and the raw relative motion xplace reads through XInput 2 sums to what QMP sent, dx -2000 and dy 200 in 25 events, as the kernel's evdev counts it, while the pointer stays at the window's left edge. In an emulated 800x600 mode xplace's window stays 800x600 at 0,0 and the screen shows it scaled over the whole output; Wine's probe at 800x600 keeps a 1366x768 window, which GE-Proton fills with its picture scaled to 1024x768 between black bars, keeping the mode's aspect. A 64-bit and a 32-bit waveOut tone at 440 Hz through PulseAudio's OSS module reach the audio loopback, and DirectInput 8 lists the system keyboard and mouse. Of twelve such tones of 2 s, nine came whole and three had one gap of 50 to 150 ms. With Wine's own 30 ms in PulseAudio each of sixteen tones had one to three such gaps in its first 0.8 s, PulseAudio logging the stream's underruns and Wine that its next period was in the past: a sleep of 5 ms, which wakes at most 3.3 ms late on the idle system, woke over 10 ms late in 9 to 13 of 1600 tries, and up to 41 ms late, while Wine's processes started and played, the four CPUs 75 to 80 percent busy. The timed-wake follow-up below traces waits for the big kernel lock; the remaining Wine gaps have not been attributed individually.

A thread woken from a timed wait under load returns tens of milliseconds late on Rach2, where Linux returns within a few, since the woken CPU waits for the big kernel lock; the [process subsystem's Results](../../../rach2/sys/proc/Readme.md#results) give the figures. The owner left the change to the big lock for the next locking milestone. Until that milestone measures this load against Debian again, `wineio` keeps reporting gaps without failing on them, and `PULSE_LATENCY_MSEC` stays at 60: the larger stream buffer reduced the recorded Wine gaps but did not remove them. The gap assertion returns with that milestone.

## Updating

A package is a line of `layer.list` or `native.list` with its version, and the version changes when the Debian layer's snapshot does. A new version of 0 A.D. needs a new replay, recorded by `games.sh record` on the Lenovo and taken again by Linux's runs: a replay records the engine's version and plays only on the simulation that recorded it. A new umu-launcher or runtime is a line of `umu.list` with its version, URL and SHA-256, from the release's published digest or the image directory's `SHA256SUMS`; Valve keeps the runtime's older image directories for some months, so a pin outlives its directory only in a clone's cache. The image depends on the list and on every script here, so `make os-real-gnu-ext2` rebuilds the root after an edit.

## Tests

`innoextract --version` on the booted root shows that the program and its libraries load. `ARCH=x86_64 tests/run games-native` plays both replays on llvmpipe in QEMU, in a small form of 640x400 and 10 s that TCG draws in minutes, a case each, `machine.games-native.supertuxkart` and `machine.games-native.0ad`, and the race in the i386 game as `machine.games-native.supertuxkart-i386` ([tests/graphics/Readme.md](../../../tests/graphics/Readme.md#native-games)); a case passes when its game played its replay through the measured window, and keeps the frame times as evidence, since the gate on them is against Linux on the same Lenovo. That gate is [`tests/system/games/lenovo.sh`](../../../tests/system/games/lenovo.sh), which plays the three games twice each on the root's own desktop session on the Lenovo's panel, with the volume held at 1, and judges each 64-bit run's median, 90th and 99th percentiles against Linux's within 10%. The GNU family's `game_launcher` row on x86-64 checks `rach2-game --print`, including its settings, an explicit ID and prefix, and a calling shell that disabled fsync or chose Vulkan. It checks that printing creates no compatibility directory.

`tests/run games-wine`, on Linux hosts alone since it boots the `virgl` profile, runs the probes of [Wine in QEMU](#wine-in-qemu) as four cases, each a boot of the GNU root with the probes' disk: `prefix` checks that `rach2-game` makes a new prefix with `syswow64` and no `VideoMemorySize`, and that WineD3D's log reports and emulates the video memory `glxinfo -B` reads; `draw-64` and `draw-32` compare each probe's CRC-32 with Linux's; `maps` compares the bytes each preloader range has mapped in a 64-bit and a 32-bit program with Linux's. `sh tests/system/games/reference.sh OUT [ROW...]` remakes Linux's results in the Debian guest; `ref/linux.json` is its `linux.json`.

The `gpu` row runs on a machine's own GPU rather than in QEMU, as root through [`gpu.sh`](../../../tests/system/games/gpu.sh), from the probes' bundle on the data partition beside a trial root, or under Linux with the Proton `-p` names: GL and Direct3D 9 at both widths, each sum judged against a successful draw in Linux's `results.json` from the same machine (`GAMES_COMPARE`), and `tripprobe` on WineD3D's GL renderer through the route and on its Vulkan renderer through Proton with the route's settings, its time recorded and the renderer checked in Proton's log. Each draw must succeed and name the GPU even when Linux's draw failed. A Linux draw with a nonzero exit or no sum supplies neither a sum nor an adapter for comparison; a failed Linux round-trip probe imposes no requirement on that renderer. The row prints each comparison it leaves out. `gpu.sh` accepts absolute or relative paths for its output, `-c` and `-p`, and removes its temporary home on every exit, including a signal. Root makes the output directory with `trip.py --out USER PATH`, which opens each directory from `/` down by descriptor, following no symbolic link, refuses any that is not root's or that another user may write, makes a missing one root's, 0755, makes the last one and gives it to the user through its descriptor; an output directory that is already the user's is taken as it is. Root then writes nothing there: the user writes the identity and the kernel's log, which root reads from `dmesg` and passes through, and makes and removes the home. It is no case of a suite. [`trip.sh`](../../../tests/system/games/trip.sh), run the same way, times `tripprobe` on the GL renderer alone, three times by default, with the kernel's counters read at the loop's start and end, when the probe's output has its feature level line and when it has its result ([`trip.py`](../../../tests/system/games/trip.py)): the loop's wall time, `/proc/stat`'s context switches and, on Rach2, the big lock's waits and, from debugfs's `bkl/calls`, its holds by entry and its takes after a switch by the call the thread slept in, and each of the probe's threads' ticks and context switches. Debugfs stays root's alone: `trip.sh` runs the user's command under a reader of root's, `trip.py --reader LIMIT`, whose standard input is one end of an AF_UNIX socket pair; each byte the user sends is answered with one frame of `bkl/calls`, `bkl/profile` and `bkl/tick`, read afresh, at most LIMIT times, `2 * (RUNS + 3)`, two snapshots for each probe trip.py may run, after which the reader closes its end. The reader opens those three files and nothing else, and makes, renames and removes nothing; `trip.sh` makes its output directory as `gpu.sh` does. The snapshot keeps the profile's and the tick's lines whole. `trip.sh -t THREAD` has `bkl/calls` count one thread alone, by ID or name, such as `wined3d_cs`, for the runs, and puts the default back on exit; each loop's summary then gives that thread's switches away by the thread switched to, the switches the kernel counted under no thread once its 32 slots were taken, which last across the runs, and its sleeps by call and ioctl request, beside each `tripprobe` thread's run time and time ready but not running, from its `schedstat`. It then runs the loop once under `strace -f -c -w` and once with its ioctls traced, counted by request, where strace is installed, and once under `perf stat` where perf is. Each run must exit successfully, report its round-trip time and print `TRIP OK`; a failure ends the step with a nonzero status.

`tests/run games-wm`, also on Linux hosts alone, runs [`wm.py`](../../../tests/system/games/wm.py) as root in the desktop session of the GNU root, with the audio loopback, as three cases: `place` sets the output to 1366x768 and checks xplace's and Wine's fullscreen windows, the screen, the grab and the raw motion; `scaled` checks xplace in an emulated 800x600 mode and Wine's probe at 800x600; `wineio` records the 64-bit and 32-bit tones from `/dev/dsp` and checks DirectInput's devices and the event devices Wine's log names; it judges a tone by the 50 ms windows the tone fills, at least 20 at 440 Hz and at most a fifth as many at another frequency, and prints the windows a gap cuts without counting them, since a gap is a matter of when the stream's writer ran. wm.py starts the session's Weston with `--debug`, which lets `weston-screenshooter` capture the output, and checks sample points of the capture, since QEMU's `screendump` finds no surface while virgl scans out a GL resource. The scenario, `tests/cases/machine/gameswm_scenario.c`, moves the pointer, clicks and presses Escape through QMP at the runner's ready lines. In `place` it first moves the mouse once, and wm.py waits for the X server's pointer device: Weston gives its seat a pointer only at a device's first pointer event (`libweston/libinput-device.c`, lines 71 to 83), under Linux as here, and until Xwayland has the seat's pointer a grab confines nothing and the first moves reach no X client (`dev-log/upstream.md`); a desktop in use has had its first move long before a game starts. It sends each later move once wm.py has printed the kernel's count of the last, since QEMU's PS/2 mouse holds what its queue of 16 bytes has no room for until the next input event, and ends xplace's count with a click, which follows the moves through the mouse; Escape, from the keyboard, can reach xplace before the last of them.

`tests/run games-umu`, on Linux hosts alone, runs the 64-bit Direct3D 9 probe through `rach2-game --umu` in one case, `umu`, on the same payload: the first start must unpack the runtime and the second neither unpack nor download it, the probe must read back Linux's pixels, its Proton log must list the options of the same probe run directly, with `wow64` and `wined3d`, and both logs fsync and WineD3D's OpenGL renderer; the 64-bit GL probe must draw on virgl through the container's `/dev/dri` with Linux's pixels; the tone probe, run through umu and directly under a D-Bus session bus and PulseAudio on OSS that the runner starts, must be recorded through HDA's audio loopback and judged as games-wm judges its tones, by the 50 ms windows the tone fills, at least 20 at 440 Hz and at most a fifth as many at another frequency, with the windows a gap cuts printed and not counted; pressure-vessel's environment in the container must name the PulseAudio socket and the session bus it passed in; and pressure-vessel's log must hold no refused call, which it records as the `strerror` text of the errno, but those the stored Linux reference's log also holds (`umu_refused` in `tests/system/games/ref/linux.json`, which `reference.sh` writes from the same row run in the Debian guest without the sound checks).
